step1_summary.Chief complaint: Burning pain when urinating (dysuria) for a few days
Symptoms: Severity: Mild to moderate, bothersome but not unbearable
Character: Stinging pain on urination, crampy lower abdominal pain not like menstrual cramps
Associated symptoms: Slight blood in urine earlier, odd smell to urine
No fever, no nausea or vomiting, no flank or back pain, no increased urinary frequency
step1_summary.Medications/allergies: No regular medications; tried over-the-counter bicarbonate without improvement; allergic to Clindamycin (causes swelling)
step1_summary.Family/social history: No family history of kidney, bladder, or bowel issues known; 19-year-old female, sexually active with one boyfriend using condoms; lives with friends near college; student; non-smoker; social alcohol use on weekends

V: Urinary Tract Infection with possible minor mucosal bleeding: Blood in urine, dysuria, and lower abdominal pain suggest bladder inflammation and irritation.
I: Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis): Symptoms of dysuria, lower abdominal pain, hematuria, foul-smelling urine without systemic signs fit UTI.
Sexually Transmitted Infection (e.g., Chlamydia, Gonorrhea): Sexual activity with no prior STD screening, urethritis can cause dysuria and hematuria.
D: None prominent, but consider Vitamin A or other deficiency causing mucosal fragility unlikely here.
I2: Medication-induced cystitis or allergic reaction unlikely (no recent medications besides bicarbonate, no known bladder irritants).
A: Allergic urethritis or cystitis related to irritants or condom allergy unlikely but possible.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classical presentation of dysuria, suprapubic cramping, microscopic or gross hematuria, and foul-smelling urine in a young sexually active female with no systemic symptoms strongly supports uncomplicated UTI.
supporting_evidence: Burning pain on urination lasting several days
Sexually active with no prior STD screen
opposing_evidence: No increased frequency or urgency reported (though absence does not exclude UTI)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Sexually Transmitted Infection (Urethritis, e.g., Chlamydia or Gonorrhea)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Sexual activity without prior screening and dysuria with mild hematuria may indicate urethritis due to STI; however, no vaginal discharge or other classic STI symptoms reported.
opposing_evidence: No vaginal discharge or other STI symptoms (e.g. pelvic pain)
No history of previous STDs or risk factors discussed

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Patient has known IBS, which can cause lower abdominal cramping; however, pain is linked temporally with dysuria and hematuria, suggesting urinary source rather than bowel.
opposing_evidence: Pain worse on urination and presence of hematuria make urinary cause more likely
